extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, journal editors, press officers, and researchers who deal with embargoed publications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and norms about the use, enforcement, and consequences of embargoes on scientific journal articles — aimed at both media and publishing professionals. Covers what constitutes acceptable embargo behavior, enforcement options, common abuses, and practical effects on reporting and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication as appropriate culmination/prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in a peer-reviewed journal is the appropriate culmination of original research and an essential prerequisite for public discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature's guidance: talk to other researchers as much as you wish, but do not encourage or risk premature publication by discussion with the press beyond your formal presentation. Science likewise discourages prior publication in print or on the Internet; the embargo period provides sufficient time for reporters to analyze and report on complex stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should enforce embargoes and sanction violators
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusive evidence that a reporter has knowingly broken an embargo will result in exclusion from future embargoed information; authors who fail to keep manuscripts privileged risk annulment of acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science: violators excluded from future embargoed information and authors risk annulment of acceptance. Monica Bradford: violators would no longer receive advance texts unless they acknowledged misdeed with a letter of apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors may speak at meetings but should not distribute full materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists may talk to media at meetings, but should not hand out copies of the paper or slides prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science allows scientists to talk to media at meetings, but not to hand out copies of the paper or slides: 'We want the scientists to decide where they want to publish.' This aims to avoid premature dissemination while allowing some communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual-agreement embargoes (limited press access) can produce accurate coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargo arrangements crafted by mutual agreement (e.g., Asilomar 1975) — limiting press attendance to reporters who accept embargo terms — can yield extraordinarily accurate and lucid coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asilomar example: press limited to ~16 reporters who agreed to embargo, twice-daily briefings held, embargo stood firm and produced award-winning coverage; illustrates that voluntary, mutually respected embargoes can work well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should not manipulate release timing for self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving embargo/release dates to accommodate partners or to gain political advantage undermines the credibility of the embargo system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples: Nature moving an embargo up (Jefferson paternity study) and aligning releases with partners (National Geographic) reduced fairness and provoked accusations of playing politics; PNAS moving a release forward to avoid being upstaged is cited as problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes are often imposed by publications rather than mutually agreed
rubrics_metrics.description: Most embargo systems are imposed by publications on the media rather than formed through mutual agreement between scientists and reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because embargoes are usually unilateral rules set by journals, tensions arise over fairness and enforcement; workshop participants examined one mutual-agreement model vs. imposed systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals must coordinate with institutions and public relations offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should notify pertinent public relations offices of research universities and supporting agencies of embargoed releases to reduce leaks originating from those organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature's plan to notify PR offices is presented as a concrete step to limit breaches that originate from research sites, funding organizations, or societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes give reporters time to analyze complex stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The embargo period provides sufficient time for reporters to analyze and report on often complex stories behind the data, improving coverage quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science and Nature emphasize that embargoes allow better-quality reporting and meaningful public scrutiny; this benefit is a central justification for embargo use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoes are vulnerable to leaks from third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Breakdowns often result not from media malfeasance but from other organizations — research sites, funding organizations, scientific societies, or commercial partners — that disclose information early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include university/funder press releases and partners like National Geographic publishing early; such violations are harder for journals to punish than media breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of embargoes for orchestrated publicity (self-serving embargoes) is illegitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes issued primarily for self-serving reasons — e.g., to tailor release times for broadcast audiences or to promote commercial partners — are treated skeptically and often ignored by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doug Levy distinguished 'real' embargoes from self-serving ones (e.g., Sunday 6 p.m. releases aimed at network news) and argued those are often ignored; reporters may not honor embargoes seen as manipulative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small, well-defined embargo circles preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations seeking embargo protection want the circle of those who have access to be as small as possible to preserve exclusivity and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LA Times position: consider an embargo broken the instant it is apparent the news has traveled outside those who agreed; suggests minimizing the number of recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective issuance to avoid 'flood' of embargoed releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine issuance of embargoed news releases for every paper may cause reporters to toss them unread; journals should be selective to avoid overwhelming media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doug Levy criticized routine embargoed releases as likely to be discarded by overburdened reporters; Turner-Lowe reported complaints about announcements issued for immediate release and invited media to agree on practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement can include access suspension by intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party services (e.g., EurekAlert!) can enforce embargo rules by suspending access to embargoed feeds for organizations or individuals who break embargoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EurekAlert! suspended the Daily Express and several reporters for six months after an intentional embargo breach; shows how intermediaries can impose practical sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo breaches can have financial/market consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaked embargoed research can lead to stock market runs and allow privileged actors to profit, raising ethical and practical concerns about pre-release dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alliance for Aging Research breaking an embargo led to a 43 percent stock climb; other leaks to analysts resulted in significant stock price run-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals may publish electronic versions and tie embargoes to electronic appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing papers on the Internet as soon as they are ready and timing embargoes by the paper's electronic appearance (possibly with different stated hours for time zones) is a considered option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science considered this approach to manage timing and fairness in an online environment; it may clarify exact embargo timing but introduces logistical complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request apologies as condition for regaining embargo access
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a letter of apology from a media outlet that violated an embargo can be a means to penalize and restore trust before resuming advance-text distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monica Bradford's approach: violators would not get advance texts unless they acknowledged their misdeed with a letter of apology; an incremental enforcement mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters/editors should sanction journals that do not honor embargoes strictly
rubrics_metrics.description: If journals themselves play games with embargoes (e.g., leaking, manipulating dates), reporters and editors should consider sanctioning those journals to maintain reciprocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robert Lee Hotz argued reporters should sanction journals that do not hold embargoes tightly because lax journal behavior undermines the whole system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo policy should address enforcement against non-media violators
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies need mechanisms to respond when violations come from non-media parties (e.g., research institutions, funding bodies) since those are harder to punish by journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop and commentaries note that policing stockbrokers or institutional PR offices may be outside a journal's capabilities, but the problem affects embargo integrity and may require broader community action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about embargo rules and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should clearly state embargo rules and the consequences of violations so that reporters, authors, and institutions understand expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science and Nature's public statements (e.g., 'Conclusive evidence ... will result in exclusion', 'Let us know of any violation; sanctions will surely follow!') serve as models of public clarity about policy and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate enforcement intensity depending on source and intent of breach
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all breaches are equal: deliberate, known violations by reporters warrant different sanctions than inadvertent leaks or disclosures by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deliberate breaking by Daily Express led to suspension by EurekAlert!, while leaks via institutional press releases or partners present enforcement challenges and may require different responses.
